data.title: Bessent, Fed's Goolsbee divided on role of energy shock in inflation
data.description:
WASHINGTON, Nov 13 (Reuters) - US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Friday that the Federal Reserve should not hike rates because of inflation driven by an "energy supply shock" tied to the Iran war, comments made to CNBC and promptly contradicted on the network by Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee, who said price pressures were building far beyond what could be explained by high oil prices.

"I think the Fed should understand that this is an energy supply shock," while the underlying US economy is very strong, Bessent said in an interview on CNBC. "So I think that to hike too much into an energy supply shock when it's coming down, these are very noisy numbers...You know, the Fed's supposed to look into the future, not look in the rearview mirror."

Shortly afterwards, the network hosted Goolsbee, a regular guest on CNBC's morning Squawk Box show, who said that inflation was not just due to energy, but had spread to the service sector and areas like medical care that are not usually responsive to the price of oil, and was also elevated through strong demand tied to the AI data center buildout.

"I respect the secretary and I am trying to figure out the same thing he is trying to figure out, which is how persistent is this inflation? The tariff inflation and oil price shock were supposed to have gone away by now and it hasn't," Goolsbee said. "One puzzle is why have those supply shocks been as persistent as they have been. A second thing is if demand is overheating and that is contributing to inflation, that is more worrisome... Services inflation, which is probably not coming from tariffs or oil, is one of the more troubling aspects of the inflation reports we have been getting."

While not committing to a rate hike, he said the Fed "has definitely got work to do to continue to reestablish its credibility."

The two interviews highlighted competing narratives about aspects of the US economy that figured heavily in midterm elections that centered on high inflation as well as the rapid pace of an AI buildout. The Trump administration has cheered the AI boom and focused on the likely upside, while being critical of communities reluctant to host the massive data centers needed for the technology.

Like other administration officials, Bessent focused on what he sees as the oil-driven roots of current inflation and criticized the Fed for responding to it.

"I'm not going to tell the Fed what to do. I am going to say they should have an open mind," Bessent said, noting that the Fed had cut rates last year, "and now to reverse just based on an energy supply shock, a reversal in a dramatic way isn't something that I would do if I were on the Fed. But I'm not on the Fed."

Fed policymakers were open to the possibility they could "look through" supply-driven inflation at the start of the US war with Iran. But as inflation remained lodged above the Fed's target, concern about it grew, as did support for rate hikes. Research meanwhile opened a different window on the relationship between oil prices and US inflation. Because the US is an energy exporter, higher global oil prices can filter through to the economy in the form of higher corporate profits and wages, providing a source of inflation beyond supply issues that can't be easily ignored by the central bank.

Recent stronger-than-expected jobs and inflation reports have further bolstered the case for more Federal Reserve interest rate hikes, and even prompted some officials to discuss the need for a larger-than-typical half-percentage-point increase at the central bank's coming December 8-9 meeting.

"We have had signs of trouble now for several months in a row if you look at how broad-based the inflation is," Goolsbee said. "In categories that are not driven by oil prices and not driven by tariffs, you are still seeing stalled progress and in some cases going the wrong way ... That is not going away no matter what happens to the price of oil."

"Are we on a path back to 2%? My feeling right now is we are not and we've got to deal with that," Goolsbee said. "Conventional wisdom says do everything you can to prevent demand overheating," Goolsbee said, with coming data on inflation the key to whether the Fed needs a faster pace of rate increases.

(Reporting by Doina Chiacu, Katharine Jackson and Howard Schneider; Editing by Alex Richardson, Doina Chiacu and Andrea Ricci )

data.title: Betterness Expands Seed Round to $3.5 Million to Build Neighborhood Health Networks in Miami
data.description:
The first network launches at Miami Worldcenter on Nov. 15 with more than 30 local businesses, a free member app and the software those businesses run on.

MIAMI, Nov. 13, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Betterness, Inc., which builds neighborhood health networks that connect people with the gyms, studios, clinics, coaches, local brands and health services around them, today announced $1 million in additional seed financing, bringing its seed round to $3.5 million. A private investment group with deep pharmaceutical expertise led the extension. The other investors bring venture capital experience and have built companies in artificial intelligence, healthcare and blockchain.

People train, eat and recover with the businesses in their neighborhood. Their health data sits in separate apps, and those businesses run on separate tools. Most health technology stops at the app or the wearable. Betterness connects the member, the local business and the health services in one network, and Bett-i, the AI inside Betterness, works across all three.

Since its $2.5 million seed round and the launch of Bett-i in April, Betterness has moved its business customers from beta to daily operations. Locations process an average of $500,000 a year in member bookings through Betterness One. Betterness will use the new financing to grow the network one neighborhood at a time, starting with Miami Worldcenter and then Miami Beach.

"The front line of health and wellness is the small business that opens its doors every day," said Demian Bellumio, Co-Founder and Co-CEO of Betterness. "We ran Betterness in beta with exceptional Miami businesses that trusted us to go deep inside their operations and rethink how they run from the ground up. What we built with them runs their businesses today, and now we are accelerating deployment. Betterness connects everyone who helps a person live better, in the real world, not inside an app. Miami is the best city to launch it, and Miami Worldcenter is where it starts."

How the network works

For members, Betterness is a free app. Members track more than 70 sports in the app or on Apple Watch, sync Garmin, Oura and Withings devices, log meals from a photo and order lab tests across the U.S. through Quest Diagnostics and BioReference. Bett-i turns that data into guidance and builds training programs from hundreds of video tutorials for strength, Pilates and yoga. When Betterness introduced Bett-i in April, Men's Fitness asked whether it was "the most ambitious AI health product ever built."

For businesses, Betterness One puts the tools a wellness business uses today in one place. In Grow, free for every business, owners publish a Space in the Betterness app, offer perks, follow their Instagram and post with Bett-i. In Host, staff sell memberships and class packs, take payments, run schedules, bookings and check-in, and put a live heart-rate board on the screen in the room. In Coach, now in beta, coaches keep a training file for every member, and Bett-i adjusts each program for the coach to approve. With Sell, coming soon, businesses will sell products inside the app.

Members decide what each business and coach sees. Bett-i runs on the Betterness Graph, where Betterness connects each member's data, with the member's permission, to the businesses and coaches they choose. Businesses and members choose the GPT or Claude model that fits them, or connect their own AI tools through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Betterness is a HIPAA-compliant platform with strict data controls. Any health and wellness business can start free with Grow at betterness.one.

"A studio or clinic can run its entire operation on Betterness One," said Ari Katz, Co-Founder and Co-CEO of Betterness. "Its members decide what to share, under strict data controls, and the business uses that to personalize classes, programs and offers in a way traditional wellness business software never could."

Why Miami Worldcenter first

At full build-out, Miami Worldcenter is planned for up to 40,000 residents in and around it. Its weekly Night Market draws more than 60 vendors. Many are small wellness businesses. Betterness built the Worldcenter Perks program with more than 30 businesses in the district and nearby. Wynwood Padel Club offers members 20% off court bookings. SWEAT440 takes part through its Brickell and Midtown studios.

Betterness launches the network at the Miami Worldcenter Wellness Series: Feeling ALIVE on Sunday, Nov. 15, from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. More than 600 people have registered. Readers can download the free Betterness app for iPhone or Android and join the Miami Worldcenter Space today. What Betterness builds at Worldcenter becomes the model for its next neighborhoods and for other cities in the U.S. and abroad.

What comes next

Betterness will add telemedicine with licensed clinicians, prescriptions filled by licensed U.S. pharmacies when a clinician prescribes them, and a curated supplement line. Members will reach these services through the local businesses they use, and those businesses need no clinical network or pharmacy of their own.

Better Health. Better Life. Together.

About Betterness

Betterness is a Miami-based health technology company building neighborhood health and wellness networks. Betterness brings a member's workouts, sleep, nutrition and lab results into one free app, with Bett-i, the AI inside Betterness. With Betterness One, gyms, studios, clinics, coaches and local brands grow, host and coach, with selling coming soon. Learn more at betterness.ai and betterness.one. Betterness provides wellness information, not medical advice.

About Miami Worldcenter

Miami Worldcenter is a new $6 billion mixed-use destination in the heart of Downtown Miami. As one of the largest private urban real estate developments underway in the United States, the project occupies 27 acres spanning ten city blocks and offers world-class retail, hospitality, commercial and residential uses. Several phases of the project have already been completed and occupied, including three residential towers, a significant portion of the retail component, and a citizenM hotel.

Miami Worldcenter Associates serves as the master developer for the overall mixed-use development, led by Managing Partners Art Falcone and Nitin Motwani, in partnership with CIM Group, a community-focused real estate and infrastructure owner, operator, lender and developer. Together they have assembled a best-in-class development team that is currently transforming the urban core of Miami into one of the country's largest mixed-use destinations. Learn more at www.miamiworldcenter.com.
